subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, March 30, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-38, an Act respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to return to this debate. Last week, the debate centred on the question of pensions and the desire of the employees of this company to have an agreement prior to their accepting employment with the new corporation. They want such an agreement because of the potential difficulties which may face Teleglobe in the future, as well as Memotec, as its owner, due to its heavy reliance on the large loan capital on which it has based its purchase of Teleglobe.
In the materials supplied to us by the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall), there is great emphasis placed on the benefits for employees which will result from this sale. In fact, highlighted within those points are the tremendous benefits which are supposed to be received by Teleglobe employees in the transfer. Yet, it has not been possible to arrange an agreement between the Government and the employees of this company, despite the fact that they have requested meetings, suggested compromise and laid out possible alternatives they might be prepared to accept. It is a crying shame that a government which makes a commitment to privatization cannot follow that commitment through by ensuring, as is done in most parts of the world where privatizations have occurred, that an agreement has been reached with the employees of the company concerned.
In this case, the employees are prepared to take on good faith the probability of the remaining points being worked out. They have suggested to us that they would, therefore, like to see this legislation put through before the end of the present fiscal year in order that the company will have a good start as a private enterprise and not have to face significant difficulties which might arise because of complications if the sale itself were delayed.
I think that is a tremendously generous attitude on the part of the employees involved. I compliment them for putting their interests secondary to the survival of this new company.
Teleglobe Canada
However, that, of course, still leaves in front of us a great many questions with respect to the viability, sensibility, and sensitivity of the privatization of this company. We could take Hon. Members in the House through a great many different documents which raise questions, documents from disinterested parties who are not anxious to attack the Government on ideological grounds, yet see in the case of this sale a foolish step being taken which can result in some very damaging effects for the company and for the country.
I would like to put on the record some of the perceptions which I think the Canadian people should have in mind as they judge this privatization over the years ahead. I think, for instance, they should know the views of one of the employees of Teleglobe who has written to us. He writes:
I work for the time being for a Crown corporation, Teleglobe, which is about to be privatized against the good advice of many people and sectors of the economy.
He goes on to say:
I am not very optimistic about the "benefits" that this will bring to anyone, the Canadian public, employees, the telephone users, et cetera, except perhaps one or two large corporations.
That is the view of an employee of this company who has put long term service into building up the corporation and who sees it now as being sold off to the private sector without a sense of logic ever being presented by the Government as to why this corporation, with its important role, should be part of the private sector as opposed to the public sector.
I said at earlier stages in this debate that this particular privatization demonstrates as well that the Government, having decided to act, could not even get its act together and do the job properly. We have enquiries taking place about insider trading with respect to Memotec's stock. This is taking place not only in one stock exchange. It is being looked at in the Toronto Stock Exchange, the Montreal Stock Exchange by the Ontario Securities Commission. We also have investigations undertaken by the federal Government itself with respect to insider trading. It has been a botched privatization in which clearly there have been people who seem to have had prior knowledge that Memotec, very much an outsider, would receive the right to purchase Teleglobe and, as a consequence, would see its shares go up significantly. That is what insider trading is all about, the purchasing of shares prior to a public announcement such as this. When Memotec was announced as the purchaser, of course, its shares did go up and those people benefited significantly.
I think as well we have to look at the question of Memotec itself. Memotec is not a large company. It is not a company which is experienced in telecommunications. Independent analysts in Toronto such as Nigel Allen suggest that if interest rates were to increase by even a quarter of a percentage point it could take a big chunk out of Memotec's equity. Other people have made the same point. This is an important public firm which handles our telecommunications with the entire world, and which works not just with other private companies but very much with public agencies in other countries. A private purchaser will, in a curious way, sit as our public

March 31, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
representative, despite the fact that it is a private firm, and as part of many of these international agencies which govern telecommunications. Despite that public role, the company has been sold to the private sector.
I refer Hon. Members to the assessment of The Globe and Mail of the process by which this sale was initiated. Lawrence Surtees writes in the business section of The Globe and Mail that the Teleglobe Canada sale is a question of act first and think later. I think that anyone who has sat through, some of the sessions of the legislative committee which heard witnesses, as I did, would have to say that there are a great many questions which remain unanswered with respect to this sale. There are questions, for instance, which were brought to us by the head of the CRTC. I tell Hon. Members that it is a pretty rare occasion when the head of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission has to come to a committee and publicly criticize a Bill which deals with telecommunications, first, because he has not been consulted sufficiently and, second, because the context of the Bill and the content of it are, in his view, dangerous to the future of CRTC regulation in Canada.
Teleglobe Canada is a company which in 1986 made for the people of Canada almost $32 million, which is a great deal of income. In 1985 it made over $33 million. This is money that went directly to the taxpayers of Canada to reduce what they had to contribute and pay to the Government. Teleglobe is a company which all taxpayers have paid for over the years. Despite having listened to witnesses, I cannot see the logic of selling this company off and making what should be a public firm serving Canadians, a public firm giving income back to the Canadian taxpayer. 1 cannot see the logic of selling it off except for the logic of an ideological commitment which bears no relationship to practicality, need or the concerns of the country.
As I think back to the witnesses who appeared before the legislative committee it seems to me that the thrust of the arguments which they brought forward, especially those brought forward by the employees of the company, were that they hoped very much that the company could stay public so that they could continue to do the excellent job which they have done for Canada. I would have hoped that that logic, that sense of commitment with respect to the desire of the workers to keep a good company going and to return benefits to the taxpayers would have eventually won out. It did not win out in the legislative committee. It has not won out with respect to government thinking. I think it will win out eventually with respect to the thinking of the people of Canada as they assess this faulty, botched privatization Bill which is before us today.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to read into the record a letter that was sent to the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougal!) just a couple of days ago. It states:
Madam Minister:
The Telecommunication Technical Services Association has learned that a motion on Bill C-38 was proposed to the House which implies that Teleglobe employees would have to negotiate a "compensation package" with the new employer prior to Bill C-38 coming into force.
Our Union does not support this motion and strongly opposes such irresponsible action as it may jeopardize the interests of the TTSA members and ultimately cause delays in the adoption of the Bill resulting in serious consequences for all concerned.
They go on to state that they hope that the meetings will take place in the meantime but that the Bill should certainly pass.
The amendment which is referred to in the letter was moved by the Liberal Party. In the legislative committee all along members of the Liberal Party attended and expressed their concern about one aspect of the actuarial assumptions, and so on, as part of the pension issue. So they were on to this issue early. Members of the New Democratic Party came onside later in an attempt to catch on to the coat-tails of the Liberal Party, so to speak.
In the meantime, members of the union are telling us in letters which they have sent to us that we should not do what members of the Opposition are asking us to do. Members of the Opposition now make long dissertations about many and varied aspects of the Bill. Under the protection of past service, Teleglobe employees have a wider range of options than what is generally available in the private sector; notably, normal PSSA options are, first, return of contributions; second, immediate pension; third, deferred annuity at age 60, or annual allowance at age 50, depending on the age or service; as well as a transfer of prior PSSA service to a new plan on a going-concern basis. For example, there is full provision for future salary increase, indexation and survivor benefits versus the private sector practice of transfer on a termination basis only. There is also a guarantee of maintenance of the full body of accrued pension benefits which are in place. There is also the option of accrued benefits with respect to leave in the PSSA under the continuity of employment option, which is similar to the private sector practice. The pension transfer provisions that these employees are looking at are tremendous. They know it. They want the Bill passed before the end of the month. The employees are telling us that we should pass this Bill, and we should heed their words.

March 31, 1987

disastrous government. This would include wiping clean the slate with respect to privatizations which, to my mind, like this privatization, have been badly botched and have been most unfortunate for Canada, not just for the employees involved.
If the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton had wished to give the full flavour of the letter to which he referred he might have read it all. In the letter it is indicated that there are still some points of disagreement that the employees of the company have with respect to the pension arrangements which have been made.
I wish to point out to the Members of the House, and to people across the country, that we are not simply talking about minor issues here; as we heard from the Treasury Board officials who appeared before the legislative committee, what we are talking about is a difference of approximately $7 million insofar as the funding of the pension plan is concerned, and that amounts to something close to $10,000 per employee. So, it is a significant factor.
As a last point, let me say that while I respect the generous decisions which the employees of the company have taken- and we shall not be holding the Bill up-that is no reason not to put before this House and before this country some of the botched efforts which have gone into privatization in this particular case and some of the sad results which may well ensue for taxpayers right across this country.

I could not help but reflect upon the discussions and debate that took place some time ago when the Government was in the process of privatizing de Havilland through a sale to Boeing Corporation. At that time, both in the House and in committee, there were many bleak predictions about what the future would be for that corporation, what the future would be for its employees, and what the future would be for the technology involved.
As we all know, Mr. Speaker, all of those predictions have proven to be incorrect. All of those predictions appeared at the time-and I think events have proven this-to be based upon adherence to ideology and a resistance to change, and the desire to make all Canadians public servants of one sort or another. I think today in this debate we are witnessing more of the same. Teleglobe Canada
having to pay and because de Havilland would prove to be extremely profitable and extremely beneficial for Boeing.
The money of which the Member speaks so glowingly could be money coming back to the people of Canada, to the taxpayers of Canada, who put so many billions of dollars into de Havilland. Instead it is money which is going to the United States in the form of yet further benefits for Boeing.
It would seem to me in fact, Mr. Speaker, that the member's argument proves our point and not his point, our point being that Boeing Corporation was going to get a Christmas gift with bells on it and keep receiving benefits of immense proportions for years on end. That is precisely what has happened because this excellent company, de Havilland, was sold to a private U.S. company, a company which is now benefiting so tremendously.
As a last point, Mr. Speaker, let me quote from the letter with respect to the pension plan. I shall put on the record the sentence which the Member for Sarnia-Lambton did not. It is as follows: "Some issues relating to transferring values for past service, in our opinion, are still not resolved." That is the reality. I think it is a sad reality. Privatization is taking place without a key question such as that being resolved.

March 31, 1987
Canagrex

The House resumed from Friday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wise that Bill C-2, an Act to dissolve Canagrex and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There were six minutes remaining in the question and comment period on the excellent speech of the Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray).

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) a question concerning Canagrex. First, I point out to you that one of the requirements for being allowed into the Speaker's Gallery in the House is that one must wear a tie.
Does the Hon. Member for Windsor West believe that the Conservative Government perhaps made a mistake in 1984 when it cut all funding to Canagrex? Did it make a prejudgment on the results of the work commenced by the Crown corporation? Does he think that is what happened? Or does he think that this was an intentional move by the Government to try to satisfy, perhaps, some objections from the United States with respect to Crown corporations in Canada? Why does he think the Government cut off its funding in 1984 and only two years later tried to do away with the Crown corporation?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do want to answer the question. However, I also want to seek your guidance, Mr. Speaker, on whether I should raise a point of order about the lack of a tie being worn by the Speaker when occupying the Chair. I will seek your guidance about this very interesting point because one cannot say that the tabs worn by the Speaker are the equivalent of a cravat. I will seek your guidance, Mr. Speaker, and reserve my right to raise a formal point of order on this subject.
Dealing with my hon. friend's question, one would have thought it would have made a lot more sense for the Government to give Canagrex a reasonable period of time to see just what kind of business it could generate for the Canadian agrifood sector, which would not otherwise have been there, before it proceeded to choke off its funding and rush legislation into the House to kill Canagrex.
It is my information that at the time the Government withdrew funding from Canagrex, it was in the process of formalizing some $100 million in export sales of Canadian agricultural products, both processed and unprocessed. These sales would not have been there had Canagrex not been able to step in and seek out opportunities in world markets. There is no doubt in my mind, therefore, that the foolish step taken by the Government to eliminate the funding of Canagrex and to kill that organization was done prematurely. It would have made more sense to respond to the views of many in the private
sector and give Canagrex a chance to show what it could do before making a final decision about its future.
The decision the Government did take was not only premature, it was foolish. The result was to lose opportunities for sales of Canadian agricultural products abroad in the area, initially, of likely $100 million, and over time perhaps in the billions of dollars. The effort by the Conservative Government to kill Canagrex has been another $1 billion mistake. The way the Conservatives bungled the matter of the failures of the two banks has cost taxpayers $1 billion. This Bill with which we are being asked to deal today represents another mistake which may well cost taxpayers, the Canadian private sector and the agri-food business perhaps another $1 billion or $2 billion.
It is a shame that the Government has taken this action. As I said before in answer to my hon. friend, we are going to make sure the Government's action is not forgotten by the voters. They will have the final say. I am confident their say, through their votes, will be that the Government made a terrible mistake, but the voters will not be making a mistake in getting rid of the Government for this $1 billion error.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) that this will be another $1 billion bungle by the Conservative Party. It is amazing to see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) sit back and allow his Government to shaft the farmers of Canada. I cannot understand that. I was in his riding on Friday night and people there are wondering why he does not stand and defend Canagrex. I was in Kindersley and the people there are so angry that from a small New Democratic Party fund raiser of 120 people we raised over $5,000. That shows you the concern those people have that the Cabinet Minister is not doing his job, and we have many good farmers who want to run in that riding. I think the only people who will win in the west now are New Democrats. I am just reading the polls.
It is very important we keep Canagrex because of competition now between the Europeans, the EEC and the Americans with their farm Bill. It is very important that we get out there and hustle to find markets for Canadian food products. I cannot understand why the Government would get rid of an agency which could do just that. The Hon. Member for Windsor West was a member of the previous Government. He and his Government knew a number of years ago that there was getting to be more and more competition in terms of sales and markets for Canadian farm goods. Why on earth did the Hon. Member's Government take so long to bring in Canagrex in the first place? Why did it wait until the dying days of a Liberal regime, until the last gasp for breath, before it introduced Canagrex to try to get a few more votes from Canadian farmers? Why was the Liberal Government so slow. It was almost slower than the Conservative Government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the original concept, I have to admit, created some controversy. There
March 31, 1987

were concerns in the private sector, both on the part of producers and processors of agricultural products, that the original concept would overlap activities already going on, and would take away opportunities which could be carried out by the private sector.
I think the parliamentary process did its job. Through the debate on the Bill at second reading, through the committee hearings and through consideration of the report of the committee, we were able to develop a concept which eliminated almost all of the concerns of the private sector and there was as a result a consensus that Canagrex, as it was passed by this House, was a good idea and deserved the support not only of this House but of the agricultural sector of Canada generally. I, therefore, say that I do not think that we took too long. The parliamentary process did its job, eliminating issues and problems which the community outside of Parliament saw in the Bill.
I think the real mistake is the mistake we are now trying to stop the Government from making by proposing this Bill. It is a mistake of the Government to try to kill Canagrex. If there was any mistake on the part of the previous Liberal Government, it is that we could not see how such an obviously good idea as Canagrex would not be accepted and would be rejected even by a Conservative Government. We thought that if it happened that we would not be returned after the next election, even the Conservatives would be able to see what a good idea Canagrex was. We could not anticipate they would be so foolish as to reject this very good idea.
In this respect I have to admit we were wrong. However, I am sure the Canadian people will assist in helping make sure these kinds of mistakes are not made again, and I refer to the mistake in judging just how foolish and lacking in understanding and intelligence Conservatives can be. I am sure that after the next election they will not have the same chance they have now to do the damage they are doing to the Canadian agricultural sector and to the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to say a few words about Canagrex because I was very closely involved with the development of Canagrex. As the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) suggests, it was a product of the past Government. It was also a product which was supported by the Conservatives in opposition. In fact, during the time of the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) brought in legislation almost identical and was ready to have it pushed through the House. Somehow between that time and when it finally got to the House four years later, the Conservatives had decided they could make it a political football. What they did was-and I can only think of one word-disgusting in its approach. They took what was a good idea, what they themselves had supported, and made it look like something which was not worthwhile.
Canagrex
Canagrex was born out of neglect, out of the neglect of many Byears of governments which did not put into place the type of marketing and exporting system which would work well for the agricultural producers of Canada. It was created because a developmental policy that would allow the continuing increase of exports around the world was not forthcoming. It was built to fill a vacuum, in spite of the fact that the Department of External Affairs said that it had in place around the world agents who would do the type of work that was necessary to increase the agricultural export market. They had not done it, and they did not do it. Consequently, Canagrex was created to fill a vacuum.
It would be of interest to review for a few moments exactly what Canagrex did put in place in its short life span of eight months. Canagrex was born on July 3, 1984. Immediately, it set out a corporate plan which touched on those areas in which it thought it could be the most effective in terms of the export of agricultural products around the world. This plan was approved by its board of directors and by the Minister of Agriculture of the day. The plan included a great number of developmental ideas. By June its plan was pretty much under way. It had a team of people in place which was working not only in Canada but around the world to develop markets and to establish a basis for realistic proposals which were put forward in the corporate plan. It found a tremendous amount of interest in the agricultural community for its plans. Producers of almost every type of product other than those already handled by marketing boards, such as wheat and grains, were interested in having for themselves some type of an agency which would develop export markets for them.
Canagrex did not go out to sell goods or to buy goods. In fact, it did not have the right to do so under the legislation. What it did was leave buying and selling to the private sector. Its objectives were to facilitate sales and to provide information to the producers and shippers of agricultural products. It surveyed Canadian commodities and found that many of them could be produced in surplus and could be sold on the world market. It also went out into many countries to find out what products they might want to buy. In the process, a source list of Canadian products, of commodities, was developed. It is probably the most comprehensive and most up-to-date source list of agricultural products that are available in Canada for sale even up to this date. I point out to Hon. Members that Canagrex was created about three years ago.
The next step Canagrex took was to develop a market survey program. This program entailed in-depth research of specific markets around the world, markets which were considered to be promising in countries which were most interested in buying Canadian products. When Canagrex went out to investigate these markets it took with it producers from each of the product areas concerned. For instance, when it went to Singapore it took pork producers along. When it went to Cuba it took potato producers along. When it went to Egypt it took along tobacco producers. In each case Canagrex used the

March 31, 1987
producers and the distribution industry in such a way so as to give them direct contacts with buyers. Many countries in the world have central buying systems. These countries practically demanded a central selling system from Canada. That is a role which Canagrex could have fulfilled, although it was not the basis of its initial mandate.
Canagrex also developed programs for the Philippines, Colombia, Panama and other South American countries. It prepared a comprehensive study that identified the markets for a number of commodities that were available. For example, it prepared a comprehensive study of markets for pork, a study which was developed in conjunction with pork producers. Commodities were listed and a potential sales list was sent out to producer organizations around Canada.
In the short time in which I have been speaking I have mentioned a number of countries. I wish to point out that if we take a look at a list of those countries to see which ones have so-called agricultural people in our External Affairs offices in those countries we will find that a number do not have any agricultural people. Consequently, nothing has developed since the days of Canagrex in terms of sales to these countries.
Canagrex was developed in such a way that most of its operation costs would be defrayed by the sale of products. The only costs of the operation of Canagrex which would be referred back to the Government, or which would become a government expense, were those with respect to the employees on its staff and the sending out of information.
After Canagrex had surveyed the markets and pin-pointed them, it then went out to stimulate export sales in the countries which it identified. It did this in a way which no commercial officer who has been posted abroad could possibly do. No agency of the Government which is not specifically interested in agriculture could have done this. To illustrate my point, Canagrex transported high quality breeding swine stock to Italy for show to ascertain whether or not Italy was interested in that type of market.
Mr. Speaker, I see you indicating that it is almost one o'clock. I will continue my remarks later on today.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF MOTORISTS-MEASURES GOVERNMENT WILL TAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Transport Canada had an excellent idea last week when it held a public forum on March 25 and 26, on restraint systems in cars.
I attended the forum and was delighted to see the positive attitude shown by all parties either directly or indirectly concerned with finding better ways to protect automobile users against highway accidents.
A number of participants stressed the importance of educating the public to increase the rate of seat belt use. A coroner who spoke to the forum pointed out that there was a right way and a wrong way to wear a seat belt.
Finally, car manufacturers announced that installation of rear shoulder belts in the back and air bags in the front would be complete by 1990.
Much remains to be done, and we will have to keep up the pressure, Mr. Speaker. The organizers are to be commended for the tremendous success of this forum, and I am anxious to see the measures the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) will introduce to ensure that the Canadian car user will have maximum protection against highway accidents.

Mr. Speaker, recently the Calgary Sun had a write-in campaign for the reinstatement of capital punishment, entitled "Let Brian Know".
As the Calgary Sun promised the petitioners, it would be hand delivered to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). After finishing my statement, I shall do so on behalf of the petitioners.
I feel more confident now that we have the promise of the Government to have a debate and a free vote on the reinstatement of capital punishment before June 1. I feel more confident, too, that this issue is going to be resolved to the satisfaction of the majority of Canadians.
March 31, 1987

Mr. Speaker, this week Pope John Paul II visits Chile, where he will become familiar with the terrible human rights situation in that country.
The Vicariate of Solidarity, sponsored by the Catholic Church, has documented hundreds of cases of torture, kidnapping, and murder. Sadistic torture methods sometimes reach new levels of technical sophistication. At other times, as in the burning of Carmen Quintana, who came to Canada for healing, they reflect old fashioned brutality.
During his visit the Pope will see a fascist Government, will see all of the trappings of power; but he will also see the courageous spirit of the Chilean people, who refuse to accept dictatorship and who continue to work and struggle for a return to democracy and freedom. I say, let the spirit of the Chilean people live and triumph.

maintopic: PETRO-CANADA PRIVATIZATION RECOMMENDED BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL OF CANADA
PETRO-CANADA PRIVATIZATION RECOMMENDED BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after careful consideration and detailed study, the Economic Council of Canada, under the eminent chairmanship of Judith Maxwell, has concluded as follows:
We recommend that Petro-Canada be privatized. The corporation should be
sold through a broad share offering, made initially only to Canadians, but no
specific legislative restriction should be placed on individual shareholdings.
Since the passage of the Petro-Canada Act in 1975, this Crown corporation has become the largest refiner-marketer in Canada. But there is no indication that the public is better off by one cent than had previously been the case.
It is time that this most sensible recommendation of the Economic Council of Canada was acted upon by the Government.

subtopic: CANADIAN COALITION ON ACID RAIN-TELEGRAM SENT TO PRIME MINISTER
CANADIAN COALITION ON ACID RAIN-TELEGRAM SENT TO PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain has urged Prime Minister Brian Mulroney to press, at next week's summit, for more substantive American actions to fight acid rain.
The Prime Minister "should ask U.S. President Ronald Reagan to submit a formal legislative proposal to Congress that would actually reduce acid rain emissions", the Coalition said in a telegram to the Prime Minister.
The telegram, signed by the Coalition's 55 member groups and 900 individual supporters, was sent Monday. A copy was released today. Coalition Co-ordinator Michael Perley said that the Prime Minister's statements on acid rain have indicated Ottawa is satisfied with Reagan's commitments, which amount to little more than research. "This impression needs to be corrected and a clear message sent to U.S. legislators and the American public that nothing short of emission reductions will solve the acid rain problem", Mr. Perley said.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Sunday morning in Quebec City, Liberal Party Members had the honour and the privilege of brunching with their Leader, thanks to modern computer technology.
Initially, the organizers were going to set up 100 tables, but because of low attendance, they reduced this number to 60.

subtopic: DE HAVILLAND-INCREASE IN EMPLOYMENT FOLLOWING PRIVATIZATION
DE HAVILLAND-INCREASE IN EMPLOYMENT FOLLOWING PRIVATIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Government decided to sell de Havilland, the opposition Parties predicted that privatization of the corporation would result in the loss of jobs. Further, they argued that the Government had destroyed a major portion of our aerospace industry.
The doomsayers on the opposition benches have been proven wrong again. Since the sale of de Havilland to Boeing, employment has risen from 4,400 people to 5,200 people, an increase of 800 jobs.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO U.S. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR'S PROPOSED LEGISLATION ON ACID RAIN
OPPOSITION TO U.S. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR'S PROPOSED LEGISLATION ON ACID RAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain has rightly sent a message to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) critical of the impression he has given to the American administration, the Congress, and indeed the American public that Canada is somehow satisfied with what President Reagan has committed himself to do so far. But things continue to go from bad to worse. We learned yesterday that Democratic House Leader Robert Byrd from Virginia is intent on weakening what is already an abysmally weak proposal by the President. Mr. Byrd is a Democrat, and so with respect to our hopes that action will come from the United States on acid rain we find that we have staunch opponents on both sides of the Congress, something that all members should regret.
I asked the Prime Minister yesterday whether he would consider asking President Reagan to assure us that he would veto any such congressional action. That kind of action has become less likely as a result of Senator Byrd's statements. I wonder whether the time has not come for all of us here in the Canadian House of Commons and in the Senate to get together to pass a unanimous resolution sending a message to the United States Congress, both the House of Representatives and the Senate, saying just how unanimous we are that the United States must take real action to reduce acid rain emissions and become the good neighbor that it says it is.

Mr. Speaker, the Special Committee on Child Care presented its much awaited report to this House yesterday. The committee was asked to report on three related subjects: the needs of children being cared for inside and outside the family, how best to define a role for the federal Government in child care, and what steps the federal Government could take to fulfil this role.
The federal Government has 120 days to give a sensitive, caring and thoughtful response to the committee's report and its 39 recommendations. I am confident that most Canadians will be supportive of the Government's response. On the other hand, I believe the knee-jerk reaction by some Members of this House and leaders of other groups in the public sector is irresponsible and smacks of blatant political posturing.
I intend to read the entire report over the next few days, and I would encourage some of the most vocal critics to do
likewise, unless they fear that a more thorough understanding and knowledge of the facts, the intensive research and well thought out recommendations, including an appreciation of the funding requirements, might alter their preconceived opinions.

CLOSURE OF A. GOLD & SONS-EARLY RETIREES-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAM

Mr. Speaker, I have a number of letters from people in my riding who are aged 55 and who lost their jobs because A. Gold & Sons have closed their doors. In their situation they were entitled to early pension benefits until August 17, 1986. Once these employees have used up their 52 weeks of unemployment insurance they will be without jobs or early retirement benefits, and they are now wondering how they will manage to keep their children in university and provide for family needs.
The Conservative Government put the axe to the early retirement program and today still, after many months, it has not announced a replacement project. These people are quite worried, Mr. Speaker, and we urge the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) to unveil his program immediately.

Mr. Speaker, like my colleague, the Hon. Member for Beauce (Mr. Bernier), I would like to draw to the attention of this House a recent Decima poll, released yesterday, which shows that 82 per cent of Canadians support the principles of Bill C-22.
In fact one of the questions asked was whether or not Canadians would be willing to pay higher prices for their prescription drugs if more research and development were done here in Canada. Sixty-five per cent of respondents said yes.
Bill C-22 is good for Canada, and Canadians support it. The opposition Parties are basing their politics on unfounded fear of vastly higher prices, but they have failed to address the important issues of better health care and intellectual property protection, values that Canadians support.
This poll indicates that Canadians do support research and development and Bill C-22. It is a Bill which, with the establishment of a drug prices review board, will provide

subtopic: MARINE ECOLOGY LABORATORY AT BEDFORD, N.S.
MARINE ECOLOGY LABORATORY AT BEDFORD, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my sincere disappointment with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) for his decision to close down the marine ecology lab at the Bedford Institute of Oceanography in Nova Scotia. There can be no sensible reason to dismantle this world-renowned facility, a facility that has proven its worth many times over since it was created.
How can the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, with the silent approval of the Government of Nova Scotia, make this decision? This amendment, known as Motion No. 2, which includes definition of research really stems from our deliberations at committee stage. It should be noted that we are dealing with a piece of legislation which fundamentally alters the way that Canadians and industry will have to respond, if you will, to the whim of the Government in the United States. Bill C-22 is not a product of any Canadian Government, it is a product of the American Government and American multinationals which

have told their branch plant economies here in Canada that they have to adhere to policy which has been developed in Washington, New York, Philadelphia and other places.

We have heard time and time again the Minister extol the virtues of Bill C-22, particularly with regard to research and development, but he fails miserably to include a direct reference to the concept in the definition in the parameters of the word "research".
In making these amendments to Bill C-22, it should not be interpreted by Members opposite, no matter how perverted their thinking may become, that we agree with the thrust and substance of the Bill. We do not agree with the Bill, and I want to make that perfectly clear.

It should be noted that there are a number of questions about the omission of the word "research" from Bill C-22 that ought to be put on record. Why has the Government refused to table the $1.4 billion commitment allegedly made by the multinationals to the Government in exchange for greater patent protection? Why is there no provision in the legislation referring to the commitments made by the multinationals and no enforcement by the board if the multinationals refuse to live up to their commitments? How will Canadians be assured that more jobs, growth, et cetera, will be created by this legislation when Canada has the most favourable research development tax incentives of any country in the world but Singapore? How will Canadians

The Government has done nothing. It has listened time and again to the multinational corporations, to corporate interests from the United States, as opposed to the Canadian industry and the sick, the elderly, the disabled and the four million Canadians who would prefer to have a definition of research in this particular Bill.

speechtext: The Hon. Member is one minute over the time he was allotted. However, I think I will give the Hon. Member the courtesy of 30 seconds so that he may conclude. Hon. Members may speak for only 10 minutes at this stage.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief because I certainly would not want to extend my time, although I know Hon. Members opposite would like to hear what I have to say.
Let me conclude by saying that there is a great deal of support in Canada for research and development. I think it is important that government Members recognize that, notwithstanding the fact that multinational corporations seem to be pulling the strings, Canadians want to see more research and development taking place in Canada. By omitting the word "research" from this legislation, government Members have made the Bill fall far short of the expectations of Canadians and Members of Parliament regarding research.

Mr. Speaker, we must face the fact that when this Bill is passed it will substantially increase what Canadians pay for the prescription drugs they need. Before 1969 we paid the second highest prices for prescription drugs in the world. Since 1969 we have had among the lowest costs for prescription drugs in the industrialized world. That was brought about by amending the Patent Act in 1969 with regard to prescription drugs. That amendment allowed the company which researched and developed a drug to recoup its costs after which generic drug companies could get a licence, pay a royalty, and duplicate the drug. When prescriptions are filled with generic drugs there is a 50 per cent or greater saving than when they are filled by brand name drugs.
We are talking about a lot of money. Professor Eastman of the University of Toronto, who did a major study on this issue in the last couple of years, pointed out that in 1983 Canadians saved S211 million by having prescriptions filled with generic products. This Bill will give the company which develops a drug an extra six years of exclusivity during which time no other company will be able to duplicate the drug or compete
March 31, 1987

pricewise. Dr. Eastman points out that as a result of this the multinational companies which develop the drugs will be able to charge as much as they want and that Canadians will pay a great deal more.
We must keep in mind that because of the revolution which has been going on in the fields of biotechnology and medical research prices for the drugs which have been coming on the market in the last year or so are substantially higher than they had been before. As I said, we are talking about a great deal of money.
Nothing is more important with regard to this Bill than the definition of "research" and what can be done under its terms in this country. Surprisingly, for all its claims about what Bill C-22 will do to advance research in Canada, the Government has chosen not to define "research" for the purposes of this Bill. A number of witnesses who appeared before the parliamentary committee in support of this Bill expressed their belief that the Bill was deficient in that the term "research" was not more clearly defined. I will mention a few witnesses who made that point. They include the representatives of Cangene, a company which is highly involved in the most modern techniques in biotechnology. The Canadian Medical Association, which has supported the principles of this Bill, made it clear that the term "research" had to be defined. Dr. Gerry Karr, a member of the board of directors of the Canadian Medical Association, made it clear in answer to questions that he believed that the term "research" had to be much more clearly and precisely detailed in this Bill.

The Governor in Council may make regulations defining, for the purposes of

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few very short comments on Motion No. 2 which is now under consideration and which would add to Bill C-22 a provision containing a clear and specific definition of the word "research". The motion moved by my colleague the hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) reads as follows:
""research" is exploratory and innovative work undertaken on a systematic basis towards the acquisition of new knowledge in new ways. New knowledge involves the integration of newly acquired information into existing hypothesis, the formulation and testing of new hypothesis or the re-evaluation of existing observations;"
To me, Mr. Speaker, this appears to be a clear, specific and adequate definition which for many Canadians may indeed be one of the reasons why Bill C-22 must be amended.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill contains definitions and measures which the Canadian public must be able to understand. It is important that Canadians know that this Bill may have a hard and very direct impact on the price of drugs.
One of the reasons given by Government Members to take action and try to amend the Patent Act is that they want to promote research in Canada, or so they say. According to their statements and their definition, the multinationals would spend close to $1.4 billion-that is 1,400 million dollars-on research in Canada.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, the former Liberal Government commissioned the Eastman report. It was tabled and led to amendments to the Patent Act. In his report Mr. Eastman pointed out that the multinationals had not invested any more than they had to in Canada, that as a rule many of those companies treated our country as a branch plant, if you will, and that very little money was invested in pure and applied research in Canada.
As a result the money of Canadians, the admittedly huge profits of these multinationals end up in foreign countries, mostly in the United States. They are spent on research and development in the United States, so the new jobs are created in the localities where the companies have their head offices. To a certain extent we too benefit from this research, but not from the economic fallout of research work done here in Canada. Now the Government is telling us: Well, you can expect $1.4 billion worth of commitments if we pass Bill C-22. This Government has been making strong statements, Mr. Speaker, but never did the companies make any kind of firm commitment with respect to research. This is why we want to define the word "research" just so people will begin to understand that we aim to ask the companies to carry out research and development projects here in Canada so as to create jobs in this country and boost our economy.
Mr. Speaker, this is all I wanted to say. I suggest it is altogether appropriate and normal that the Government accept to amend Bill C-22 and include a clear and specific definition of the meaning of the word "research", and I commend the Hon. Member for moving this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to speak to this amendment. We oppose Bill C-22 because it is negative legislation that is damaging for Canadian people and will result in higher drug prices. This Bill is a result of the cave in of the Government to the demands of the U.S. pharmaceutical industry and to the American Government which is largely under the influence of that industry.
We know that we cannot make a bad Bill good by amending it, but we hope that perhaps some amendments can build fences to remove some of the more damaging aspects of the Bill.
That is why we are very anxious to see some definition of research. We do not believe that the amendment moved by the Hon. Member from the Liberal Party goes far enough, but it is still a beginning. We do not want to leave the definition of research to the regulatory process which is hidden away and has no accountability to the House.
Therefore, given the need for a definition of research and that even the Canadian Medical Association in its appearance before the committee stressed the need for a stricter definition, why did the Government not introduce such a definition of research? Why does the Government leave it up to the Opposition to define something as basic to this Bill as that? In fact, in other legislation the Government provides a definition.
For example, Section 2900 of the Income Tax Act defines scientific research for the purposes of the Income Tax Act. Not only does it have a positive definition, it also has a negative definition, part of which I would like to read into the record. It says that scientific research:
-does not include activities with respect to
(d)	market research or sales promotion;
(e)	quality control or routine testing of materials, devices or products;
(f)	research in the social sciences or the humanities;
(g)	prospecting, exploring or drilling for or producing minerals, petroleum
or natural gas;
(h)	the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or
product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
(i)	style changes; or
(j)	routine data collection.
Such things as market research or sales promotion, or style changes, or routine data collection are not allowed in the definition of research according to the Income Tax Act. I suggest that they should not be allowed in this Bill. But we do not know what is going to be allowed. Why does the Government not come out and say what its definition of research is? I suggest it is clear that the reason the Government rejected the Income Tax Act definition is that the pharmaceutical manufacturers want to include expenditures of this kind in areas such as applied research, market research and style changes. That is simply not good enough.
March 31, 1987

The Government has promised that there is going to be basic research. We have a great many concerns as to whether or not that is really going to happen. Dr. Lexchin has characterized the way in which applied research takes place in the drug industry, and I would like to quote from his comments. He said:
Much of the applied research and development that is carried out by Canadian companies is done for one of two reasons: either to take advantage of tax concessions, or to satisfy the Health Protection Branch's regulations about clinical testing of new drugs. Applied research and development also assumes a highly routine character, which tends to make these tasks unappealing to university scientists. Furthermore, in a profit motivated Firm there is always a latent conflict between an atmosphere of freedom, which is necessary for good scientific endeavour, and the necessity of direction from those who are responsible for the conduct of the firm.
When applied research and product development are the predominant research activities, both the goals and procedures become relatively well defined, and an atmosphere of completely free inquiry is not crucial. These considerations may explain the fact that although the pharmaceutical industry provided approximately 21 percent of the total funds for health care research in 1977, it utilized only 11 percent of the total number of medical researchers in this country in that year.
In other words, the pharmaceutical industry is not oriented toward the kind of basic research the Government would have us believe from some of the comments made by government Members in the debate so far. It is interesting that even the Canadian Medical Association, which has supported the PMAC in its desire to have changes, has said in its brief, and I quote:
It is our opinion that additional measures are required to encourage investment and high quality research ... In order to achieve this goal it will be necessary to define more precisely the term Research and Development as it applies to C-22.
On page 8, the CMA, as one of its three recommendations, adds:
That a precise definition of research and development be established for the purposes of interpreting and administering Bill C-22.
This is from a supporter of the Bill. When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) asked:
Do you believe that the section in the present draft legislation is deficient, in that it should be much more specific as to what kind of research should be considered as part of the package that the companies have promised, in terms of going to $ 1.5 billion rather than just leaving it to the companies' whim?
Dr. Gerry Karr of the Board of Directors of CME said: "Emphatically yes". For these reasons I would very much want to say that either the definition proposed by my Liberal colleague should be accepted or the definition which is proposed in the later amendment of my colleague, the Hon. Member from Winnipeg North, should be adopted. I think it is absolutely essential that we not leave this Bill completely defenceless and open with respect to the question of what "research" involves. We should not leave that entirely to the regulatory process. We as Members of Parliament, representing the people of Canada, should have a say in it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take time to speak to this motion, which was introduced by my
Patent Act
colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), defining the word "research". I think I should read that motion one more time. The Hon. Member, I might add, has done a tremendous amount of work trying to get legislation through this House that will not destroy our drug industry in Canada, certainly on the generic side, so that we can show some compassion and feeling for our poorer citizens and, indeed, for all Canadian citizens by being able to give them drugs at a cheap and affordable price. The motion states:
That Bill C-22, be amended in Clause 15 by adding immediately after line 34 at page 10 the following:
" "research" is exploratory and innovative work undertaken on a systematic basis towards the acquisition of new knowledge in new ways. New knowledge involves the integration of newly acquired information into existing hypothesis, the formulation and testing of new hypothesis or the reevaluation of existing observations;".
For the life of me, Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why the Government would try to get a Bill through this House without clearly defining the word "research". I can only think it must be trying to hide something. I have received letters and I am sure every Member of Parliament has also received a number of letters from interested individuals and groups such as senior citizen groups and groups representing the Royal Canadian Legion and all those who would be affected by paying a higher price for drugs if this legislation is passed. I have a copy of a letter written to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) dated November 24, 1986. A copy of the letter was sent to me as well as to other Members of Parliament from Prince Edward Island, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and to the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney).
We are dealing with the importance of the word "research" being defined in the legislation and not by regulation. I believe this letter is very appropriate to the motion before us today and I would like to read it into the record. It reads:
Dear Minister:
As a long-time member of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada, a former company director and member of the PMAC I can no longer remain silent regarding the issue of drug patent legislation.
Based on nearly 25 years experience in the industry and participation on numerous PMAC committees I can say without hesitation that you and your government associates are being bamboozled and indeed railroaded into a quick decision in the sole interest of U.S. protectionism.
If the legislation you are now proposing is enacted into law this country will be faced with a monstrous increase in drug costs.
This is what a man who has been working for 25 years in the industry and who understands it is saying versus the Minister who tells us there will be no extra costs for drugs. The letter continues:
With rising hospital costs and insurance premiums individual Canadians will have to dig deeper into their pockets in order to provide additional profits for the majority of PMAC members whose head offices are located in the United States. Canadians will gain nothing!
The suggestion that this country will profit from multi-millions of dollars of investment in drug research is ludicrous in the extreme. Less than 5 per cent of new drug introductions over the past several decades have been the direct result of research in the United States or Canada. The great bulk of new drugs

Adjournment Debate
introduced on the North American continent had their origins in Switzerland, Germany, Great Britain, Sweden, Norway, Italy and Japan.
Working through appointed resident research groups every major U.S. company seeks to obtain a license for new drugs as they are discovered in the countries mentioned. These, in turn, are then put into a screening and clinical research process before they ultimately appear on the North American market.
This procedure of screening and testing is indeed subject to high costs and a protracted time schedule due to U.S. and Canadian government regulations but is a far cry from the costs involved in basic research to isolate new drugs. The high costs claimed by PMAC members for "so-called" research-
This is the point at which he brings in the so-called research.
-involves a higher percentage for "clinical research" that should more appropriately be debited to merchandising. This results in highly exaggerated claims that have no relevance whatever to actual research expenditures.
That is why the word "research" should be clearly defined in the Bill.
Three companies alone in Switzerland-Ciba-Geigy, Hoffman-La Roche and Sandoz control a remarkable number of widely used prescription specialties. It is well known that Hoffman-La Roche alone earned well in excess of one billion dollars on the drug Valium which only now has come off the protected patent list. What is more important is that close to 100 per cent of the research and development facilities of these companies is located right in Switzerland. Do you seriously think that these and other PMAC member companies are going to duplicate costly research facilities just to satisfy the Canadian Government and then not raise prices on all drugs? To suggest that Canada's minuscule contribution to Valium profit will encourage greater investment in Canadian research facilities is naive indeed.
The PMAC is interested in the protection of its members. This is first and foremost. It has no interest whatever in seeing Canadians get the best of available drugs at competitive prices. Drugs, like cars, textiles, electronics or food are marketed to make money. The fact that they happen to cure some diseases or relieve pain is incidental. This is the nature of the business and if you and your government can be hoodwinked into believing otherwise then all Canadians must pay the consequences.
As one Canadian who just happens to have been close to the drug scene for many years this is how I see it. I trust and indeed hope that the legislation now in the discussion stage will be abandoned completely before it is too late.
The letter is signed by R. H. Wygant, President of Seawood Estates Inc., Prince Edward Island.
Not I, nor any Member of Parliament, could have outlined the situation any clearer than is outlined in this letter. That is why I thought it important to read it into the record. This letter was written by a man who spent 25 years as a member of the pharmaceutical industry in this country. This is a man who took the time to write the Minister and advise with respect to this legislation. This is a man who understands the industry. He is a man who happens to reside in my province right now, the Province of Prince Edward Island, who understands that it is the province in which the highest number of senior citizens in the country live. This man should be listened to. He is the man who also makes it quite clear that more than 5 per cent of the research that is done on drugs, and prescription drugs of any kind, is done either in Canada or in the United States on what he calls "basic research".
Mr. Wygant is trying to tell us that the American drug laws and the American multinational companies are trying to force
this issue, and very successfully I might add, on the Government at this time. This is a man who is trying to tell us that the only research that will be done will be done in marketing. That is what I suspected when this legislation was first talked about. I suspected that here was a way that the United States, and the large American corporations, could see a weak and vacillating Government in Canada of which they could take advantage. In this way they can move in here and exploit the poor people of this country, the aged, the sick and those on this continent who are less fortunate than probably some of the multinational corporations who are paying their presidents as much as $1 million a year.

Mr. Speaker, at long last Bill C-22 is back before the House for consideration at report stage. This Bill, which would change the conditions by which Canada would permit the production of generic drugs, is bad medicine for Canadians. It is bad medicine for our national health program. I note the arrival in the House of the Minister in charge of this legislative catastrophe. I note also that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has been here in the House throughout the initial stages of the debate on report stage of Bill C-22. That is appropriate since this Bill has a lot more to do with the
March 31, 1987

interests of a foreign power than it has to do with the Canadian people.
Earlier, I heard the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) taking wing in a flight of fancy, lofted by the vents of the PMAC poll. She was ecstatic, I suppose because she was surprised that the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association conducted a poll and found out that massive numbers of Canadians are in favour of legislation that will hurt them. She somehow found it within her naive consideration of reality that all of the previous polls, and all of the thousands of names submitted in this Chamber in protest against this legislation, were somehow misled or perhaps a sheer invention.
One searches and has searched repeatedly for reasons for bringing this legislation to Parliament. One of the reasons about which we are certain is of appropriate interest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We know the history. Ronnie and Brian got together. Ronnie said: "Brian, come on, man, we have to change this ridiculous arrangement up here in Canada which provides drugs cheap to sick people. That has to change". There are reasons for this, of course. The Government craftily negotiated a trade arrangement with the United States. It had a list of the things it wanted to give up to show its sincerity. We know the history of what has been given up in order to have nice, comfortable, friendly negotiations with the United States. Never has a Government offered so much in order to have another country buy this country cheap.
We could look beyond that for reasons which have been articulated by the Minister for wanting to pass this legislation. He tells us that he has a promise from the multinationals that they will do "oh so much research in Canada", that they will create 3,000 jobs and spend $1.5 billion by 1990-91. There are two notable aspects with respect to this matter. There was the contesting proposal from Eastman that there be legislated in a new Patent Act a mechanism involving increased royalty payments which would provide a stimulus, an inducement, an incentive, for more research by those companies, which have had up until now, it is true, a ridiculously bad record of research expenditures in Canada. That record is even worse than the average among multinational companies in other areas of manufacturing.
Having set aside a reasonable proposal, he has a promise that is not on paper. But the most absurd thing in all of this, Mr. Speaker, is that he has a promise for research and he does not even know what it is, or at least there is nothing in this legislation that tells us what it is.
To the multinationals, "research" could mean everything from basic research to studies on whether the pills should be square, round, longitudinal, or hollow.
The amendment before us is intended to help the Minister out. It at least provides a definition which will fit into the provisions for the evaluation of costs, provisions which are supposed to serve the Drug Prices Review Board. As you may
Patent Act
recall, Mr. Speaker, the Drug Prices Review Board is going to look at what the companies are charging and somehow make them adhere to some notion of "appropriate pricing".
We will not talk about how ridiculous that notion is in its fundamentals, but among the costs that are supposed to be included are the costs for research.
One would think that any normal human being, much less a Minister, would have the good sense-and even the Secretary of State for External Affairs across the way is smiling because he knows how ridiculous it is-would expect that this legislation would at least include a definition of research.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I think the amendment suggested by the Official Opposition that an attempt be made to define research is a good one, and they have taken their shot at it. I want to congratulate them for that. They at least show a little more sophistication than the Minister and the Government whose legislation this is. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the definition is somewhat flawed. Let us examine what it states. It is as follows:
"research" is exploratory and innovative work undertaken on a systematic basis towards the acquisition of new knowledge in new ways. New knowledge involves the integration of newly acquired information into existing hypothesis, the formulation and testing of new hypothesis or the re-evaluation of existing observations;-
I have been a scientist for a long time, and I can tell you that this is the kind of definition that philosophers attribute to science. There is one notable omission from this definition, and it is that it makes no reference to the fact that science is empirical, that it involves the laboratory. Unfortunately, this definition would involve as "research" history as well.
With deference to my historian colleague to my right, it may very well be that it would be useful to fund research in the pharmaceutical industry so that the Government will remember the situation that existed pre-1969, a situation which would be repeated by this Bill, and it is that the multinationals raped this country in their pursuit of profits, and all at the expense of the ill. The arrangements which were then enacted became a part of a coherent program, providing health services to all at prices they could afford.
But, Mr. Speaker, I know that you are liable to allege that I am not being serious when I suggest that there be the inclusion of history as appropriate research for the pharmaceutical industry, and so, whatever happens to this amendment, I will in fact recommend to you the proposal of the New Democratic Party in Motion No. 43, an amendment which, while it does not define research, certainly prescribes the limits that make it possible to evaluate what the multinational drug companies will be doing in terms of research.
I think that the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, will be that the Minister knows no more about research than he does about the nature of this country, when it comes to the basis of a national health program which provides service to all at an economical cost.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, am very pleased to rise on the motion introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall).
One of the major planks that the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada has used in trying to market Bill C-22 is that of the research and development spin-offs that would accrue to Canada.
In the legislation, Mr. Speaker, that comes before the House, Canadians-not scientists and not researchers, but Canadians from coast to coast-can identify with the political Party of their choice. The legislation itself helps define the differences between the various philosophies that we see exhibited on the floor of the House of Commons.
Certainly, Bill C-22 is such a piece of legislation. It is a piece of legislation that illustrates to Canadians the mind-set of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada. It is a piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker, that underlines the progress that we have made in the area of our health care system and the medicare system of this great country.
Canadians will ultimately reject this piece of legislation. We saw this in the emotionalism contained in the over-all mobilization of the senior citizens across this country when this Government tried to move on the deindexation of senior citizens' pensions.
I am not sure that what we will see in connection with this legislation will match that which we saw in connection with the deindexation of senior citizens' pensions, but it will come close. The Government simply cannot move on such pieces of legislation and not expect feedback from the Canadian electorate.
Going back to the initial response of this Government on the whole question of research, given that the Government is using the research and development argument as the major selling point in respect of this piece of legislation-a piece of legislation which ultimately will be rejected by Canadians-it is disconcerting for Canadians to learn that the Government of Canada has not even taken the step of defining what research means. This is something that goes to the very heart and soul of this legislation. The Government has not even made a commitment to ensure that the moneys that it says will flow from research and development on the part of the multinationals will in fact come about.
The amendment put forward by my colleague is an attempt to get this Government to commit itself to what it means when it speaks of research and development, an attempt to get this Government to ensure that the $1.4 billion figure that it uses in respect of the research and development expenditures that will be encouraged through this piece of legislation is in fact spelled out in black and white for all Canadians.
The Government cannot argue that this legislation will help the average Canadian in terms of drug costs; it cannot argue that this is a made-in-Canada policy. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that this policy is being dictated by the large U.S. multinational corporations. It is something that is being dictated by those south of the border.
The Government cannot argue that this legislation is in the best interests of our nation. Therefore, its only remaining argument is that of research and development; its only remaining argument is to try to show to Canadians how many jobs will in fact be created. But, this Government is not doing that, Mr. Speaker. The Members of this Government are talking about it and using it as rhetoric in their speeches across this country. But when it comes down to showing a commitment in the legislation itself, when it comes down to showing the clarity that Canadians request and require in order to begin to believe some of the things the Government is saying, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada has not had the courage to illustrate that its convictions, its rhetoric, have a basis in fact.
It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that the consumer and corporate affairs critic of the Liberal Party of Canada has tried to tie this Government down in terms of its promises to Canadians. If the Conservative Government is not prepared to be very specific in defining what it means by research and development, if it is not prepared to ensure that there will be a guarantee of the $1.4 billion in research spin-offs, it is removing the very proof that it has tried to demonstrate to Canadians in order to obtain their support for the piece of legislation. If it is removing the entire research plank, why is it continuing to put forward this piece of legislation? If it is not prepared to define its essential argument, which is the guiding light in this piece of legislation, for whom is the legislation triggered or whom will it help?
In my constituency of York West there is no support for the legislation. Last weekend I had occasion to address 400 Canadians belonging to an association of senior citizens of Metropolitan Toronto and affiliated with the Villa Colombo, an Italian senior citizens' home. This piece of legislation was at the forefront of those discussions. It was at the forefront of their concerns, concerns which we as a Parliament must begin to understand and listen to. One would have thought that the Conservative Party of Canada would have learned its lesson with its deindexation legislation.
Government Members thought that they would be able to move on what they thought was a very unorganized, unmobilized, and perhaps passive constituency. How wrong they were. Canadians discovered that the senior citizen constituency was far from being immobilized or far from being dispassionate about issues concerning themselves in a very direct way. This piece of legislation is moulded in that same regressive attitude which characterized their initial legislation on the entire deindexation of senior citizens' pensions.
It is much larger than simply the senior citizens constituency. It gets at the very essence of Canadians who are deserving of drugs. I am not referring to those who can simply afford
March 31, 1987

drugs, but those who in fact need them. Drugs should be accessible to such people. However, if we are to move forward vis-a-vis the accessibility of drugs and the affordability of drugs, we should move in a progressive way which will enhance the accessibility and affordability of drugs for all Canadians regardless of age, income, or background. That is for what the Liberal Party stands for. That is what is behind Motions Nos.
2 and 3 and the long list of amendments we proposed at committee stage.
It is time the Government began to understand where those amendments came from. Essentially, they are not amendments from an opposition Party whose sole interest is to oppose. The amendments reflect the evidence which we heard in committee. The amendments reflect the national constituency out there which is beginning to tell the Conservative Party of Canada and the Government it leads that they are mistaken in their direction, that they are mistaken in the essence of Bill C-22.
Bill C-22 embodies something which Canadians will ultimately reject. Unfortunately, Bill C-22 depicts what it means to be a Conservative, a Tory in Canada. It is our hope and aspiration that these amendments will be accepted, that these motions will be taken in the light in which they are being offered, that is, essentially speaking on behalf of average Canadians who do not want their drug costs to rise and medicine to be inaccessible to them.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of Motion No. 2 which is now before the House. It deals with the definition of research presented by the Liberal Party.
I find it very strange that in a Bill respecting research, amending the Patent Act, and abolishing generic pharmaceuticals, there is no definition of research. I find it extremely surprising, coming from the Conservative Party of Canada.
Why?

I will answer the question. I am surprised that the Conservative Party of Canada would leave the definition of research to the Cabinet, to the bureaucracy, and to the multinationals, in effect.
I remember the same Conservative Party when it was in opposition. Time and time again it said to the House, when the Liberal Party did the same thing, that we should not leave the definition of important things to regulation, to secret meetings behind the scenes, to cabinet Ministers, to their bureaucrats and staff, or to vested interest groups, be they corporations or whatever. Also it said to the House that we should have more openness in Parliament and in the country, and more participation by parliamentarians in terms of drafting regulations and defining what we mean by certain legislation which goes through the House.
I could name many pieces of legislation in the last number of years where parliamentarians meant one thing at the beginning and the meaning was entirely different at the end.

When a piece of legislation was passed and it got into the hands of the bureaucracy, regulations were made to define terms and concepts, and its entire meaning was different at the end of the process from what it was at the beginning.
I am really surprised to see the Conservative Party take one line in opposition, and now that it is in government take the other line. Perhaps it is a bit like the name of the Party. It is the Progressive Conservative Party. Its Members are a bit more progressive in opposition and a lot more conservative once they are in government.
Just like the Liberals.
