I see the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) sitting in the House this afternoon. When he was in opposition, he protested against power being given to the bureaucracy to draft regulations and power being given to cabinet Ministers to draft legislation. However, now that he is in government, he sits quietly by and, like a trained seal or a little pup, says "aye man aye". When a cabinet Minister says, "jump", he says, "how high?"
I am surprised by these long-time members who used to criticize the Government when they were in opposition for not allowing parliamentarians to have more power. Now that they are government back-benchers, they are afraid to stand and speak their mind. Why do they not have the courage of their convictions to rise in the House and say what they think? Is it because the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine believes that if he does not rock the boat he will be a cabinet Minister some day? Is that the reason? God help us if that were to occur. He does not want to make the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) angry. He does not want to make him angry.
It is surprising to see these Members, who were so vocal, sanctimonious, and self-righteous in opposition, become toothless tigers or toothless pussy-cats once they are in government. Their fangs have been pulled.
They are jellyfish.

They are jellyfish. Perhaps one of them would rise to explain why the transition took place. I am sure that it is a real disappointment to their constituents.

I wonder why the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass), the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) and the Hon. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to join in today's debate on this very important subject outlined in Bill C-204.
Smoking kills over 300,000 Canadians every year. It is the single most common cause of health problems in our society today, and it is preventable.
Before becoming the Member of Parliament for Scarborough Centre, I had the pleasure of serving as the Chairman of the Public Health Board for the City of Scarborough. During my term of office the board began drafting the by-laws for the City of Scarborough. I am very pleased to say that today those by-laws that were being drafted to promote non-smoking and encourage a healthy life-style are now in effect. The Scarborough Council recently passed a non-smoking by-law that all civic offices are now smoke-free and local establishments are subject to defined non-smoking regulations.
While there has been a recent decrease in smoking, the trend toward increased smoking among young people, especially women, is really quite discouraging. In addition to the two out of five Canadians who are smokers, there are many more involuntary passive smokers.
These people suffer many of the same health effects as smokers. Tobacco smoke irritates eyes, impairs lungs, aggravates the respiratory system, and increases blood pressure. It can also lead passive smokers to greater risk of lung cancer and one recent study showed that non-smoking spouses of heavy smokers had twice the risk of developing lung cancer as spouses of non-smokers.
Cigarette smoke contains over 50 known carcinogenics. In fact, if the toxic chemicals in cigarette smoke were taken out and dumped somewhere, they would be outlawed by the federal Government's new Environmental Protection Act. Two of these chemicals come under the classification of the Dangerous Substances Safety Standards which say: "No exposure or contact by any route, respiratory, skin, or oral, as detected by the most sensitive methods shall be permitted to these chemicals".
Non-smokers exposed to smoke are at as great a risk as smokers. A non-smoker in a smoke-laden room will inhale as
March 31, 1987

many of these carcinogenics in one hour as a smoker smoking 35 filter tip cigarettes.
Smoking in the workplace not only causes health problems but economic problems as well. Smokers take more sick leave than non-smokers. Smoking affects the morale of workers as well. In a recent survey by the Canadian Journal of Public Health eight out of 10 respondents stated that they experience physical discomfort in the presence of second-hand smoke. Lost productivity and wages due to smoking add up to over $5.5 billion every year. That is a drain on our business community and on our economy as a whole.
Comprehensive non-smoking policies which include smoking cessation programs have been implemented by Health and Welfare Canada, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Auditor General's Office, the National Research Council, the Public Service Commission, and Statistics Canada. These programs provide a model for several other federal Departments that are currently developing a smoke-free work space.
Most provincial Ministries of health have enacted some nonsmoking restrictions and several are providing support to community initiatives to reduce smoke in the workplace.
I am very pleased that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has recently proposed a new air regulation to ban smoking in Canadian aircraft for both domestic and transborder flights of two hours or less. The flights between Toronto and Ottawa are certainly much more pleasant.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has done some advertising aimed at discouraging smoking. The most recent is the Break Free campaign which is targeted at young people. This is a component of a federal, provincial and territorial initiative, the national program to reduce smoking. Moreover, there are campaigns sponsored by non-governmental organizations such as the Canadian Cancer Society and the Canadian Lung Association. A number of these organizations receive government funding for their campaigns to promote a smoke-free society.
What is the future? Given current trends, a number of directions are expected. In the matter of claims of non-smokers and smokers' rights, the trend toward according greater attention to the rights of non-smokers can be expected to continue and be extended.
Second, in the aspect of health, enhanced efforts at informing the public about the illnesses attributable to smoking and encouraging the adoption of healthy life-styles can be expected, with children and young people as major target groups.
Third, with respect to safety, it can also be expected that efforts to protect the public from the hazards from involuntary exposure to smoke will be enhanced, especially in the workplace and in public transit vehicles.
Finally, efforts to develop ways to assist those involved in the production and marketing of tobacco to switch to new enterprises in order to offset the economic losses caused by the
Non-Smokers' Health Act
declining market for their product are expected to continue over the long term.
Although the federal Government has already taken steps in addressing these issues, it plans to do more and is currently studying new initiatives with a view toward adopting a more comprehensive and health-oriented policy on tobacco. That is why it supports the spirit and the essence of this Private Members' Bill which attempts to reduce tobacco consumption and protect the public from involuntary exposure to tobacco.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in the debate on the Private Members' Bill introduced by the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). The legislation proposed in Bill C-204 would regulate smoking in the federal workplace and on common carriers other than in designated smoking rooms. Smokers in contravention of its provisions would be subject to a maximum fine of $50. Employers who failed to provide a smoke-free working environment would be liable to a maximum of $10,000. The employers envisaged by the Bill would include not only the federal Government but also Crown corporations, contractors operating under the Canada Labour Code, the Senate and House of Commons, the Library of Parliament and individual Members of Parliament.
The legislation also attempts specifically to regulate smoking on aircraft, ships, railway cars and motor vehicles which are governed by federal legislation, and it is this aspect of the Bill that I wish to address.
With respect to smoking in the workplace, I know many other Hon. Members have had a chance to speak on the subject, but as a non-smoker myself, I applaud the efforts I know my colleague has been making for so many years to encourage non-smoking throughout Parliament Hill and in our offices. It is happening. I see it around me every day. I go into committee rooms which are non-smoking. I go into conferences which are now non-smoking. The message is certainly getting across.
Before dealing with the issue of smoking on common carriers, I would like to make it clear that I am fully aware of the dangers associated with tobacco smoke to both users and non-users. My colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Browes) pointed some of those out in her previous speech.
If I have some concerns with the specific legislation prepared by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood, it is not because I disagree with her broad objectives, which are admirable, but because I think her strategy for attaining them, particularly with respect to common carriers, is costly, perhaps impractical at this point, and in some cases possibly even counter-productive. Not so.

Not so? I appreciate the information. That was the way we read the Bill, but it is certainly an offence for which there are the fines which have been indicated.
I think the problem we would still find in trying to implement this in the case of common carriers is the fact that it would be costly to try to enforce, and in the case of common carriers such as ships, enforcement would be pretty difficult at this point in time. Transport employees who provide direct service to the public often share their workplace with the public, and in large airports, ports, railway and bus stations, with private users of the facility. Those who operate the means of transport, pilots, ships crews and truck drivers, perform most of their duties in quarters which, under Bill C-204, would constitute work spaces. Depending on the particular situation, in some cases they are now indeed separate places. A truck driver usually has a cab and a ship's crew, depending on the kind of ship, will have a separate place. It might or not work out depending on the make-up of the crew in that particular kind of operation.
The Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow) spoke recently on this Bill and she had similar concerns. She dealt with some of the details of the problems associated with regulating smoking on common carriers and in transport terminals where the employees share their work space with the public. She also outlined the many voluntary self-regulating initiatives which have been undertaken by employers in the carrier industries. I am sure all Hon. Members present today are aware that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has published in The Canada Gazette for public comment before March 3, the regulations he would like to impose on smoking on passenger aircraft. As indicated, this would apply to flights of less than two hours. I think that is certainly a very laudable effort. I know that Air Canada has already initiated this ban on some of the shorter flights. I certainly appreciate that. I hope it is extended and receives public support. I believe from the indications we have received so far that the non-smoking flights have been accepted by the public, but it is being done in a gradual and progressive way.
The problem of regulating smoking in operational work spaces in all aspects of the transport sector would not perhaps be quite as easy to deal with. While the federal employer may reasonably require employees who smoke to be subject to certain restraints during normal working hours in buildings and workshops, since they are free to smoke once they leave and can be provided with designated smoking areas, operational staff do not enjoy the same liberty. I might just say that I support the Hon. Member's initiatives with respect to the concept of having separate smoking areas to which employees can go if they must have a cigarette.
The Coast Guard fleet, for example, spends more time at sea than alongside, and it would not make either legal or common sense to impose unilaterally a ban on smoking aboard Coast Guard vessels. The crew are at home when they are not on
duty and should be entitled to the same sort of freedom on their own time as are land-based employees. In circumstances such as these, the only practical approach to resolving conflicts between the wishes of non-smokers and those of smokers is a co-operative one. Differences must be dealt with in a spirit of mutual respect and understanding when people are confined to small areas for lengthy and often stressful periods of duty.
The issue of smoking and non-smoking has a long history which goes back at least to the time of James II. As far as I am aware, it has yet to be resolved. A careful study of that history suggests that persuasion has always worked better than fear or punishment as a modifier of private behaviour and a catalyst for good interpersonal relations.
I agree with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre, that the major emphasis should be on prevention. As we know, the biggest group which is still attracted to smoking are young teenage women. I am a mother of a teenage girl and we have often talked about this particular issue. As she says, everyone is going to try smoking at some point or another. It is part of growing up and part of experimentation. A lot of it relates to peer pressure and what is acceptable within a group. It seems to me that through advertising on television, through promotion in magazines and books which teenage girls read we can get the message across. I know the kinds of books teenage girls read and the message imparted is that smoking is not the smart thing to do, that we do not need to smoke to be acceptable to our peers or to be grown up. Indeed, it has the potential of a real hazard to your health. I think we could be more creative than we are now in trying to deal with that particular part of the problem.
I would like to see a much more concerted effort with respect to the prevention side of smoking and some reasonable measures with respect to the rights of smokers and nonsmokers in public places and private offices, recognizing that harsh penalties are not the way to bring about those changes.
In conclusion, while I agree with the spirit and objectives of the Hon. Member's Bill, I do not support it in all its details. I think it will make an important impact and progress towards the ultimate objective I believe most Hon. Members share, that of diminishing the amount of smoking and the costly impact of smoking on the health of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I rise happily to participate in the debate on Bill C-204, the legislation introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). I have listened very carefully to the intervention of the Hon. Member for Scarborough-Centre (Mrs. Browes) and the Hon. Member for Capilano I thought those interventions were thoughtful. I would like to confess that I am perhaps the only smoker who has participated in this debate thus far.
Smoking has a very long tradition, having begun several centuries ago. It is a habit that provided some pleasure to a
March 31, 1987

population whose life expectancy was somewhat shorter than it is today. In fact, what has happened is the discovery that as conditions of health and the environment have improved in most respects over the years, people have increased their life expectancy. Indeed, people have lived long enough to discover that some of those things that we had become used to can affect our health very seriously.
Up until now the condemnation of smoking that I have experienced has been from my wife who complains about my yellow teeth, and from my barber who tells me that my gray hair is coloured by the smoke of the cigarettes I smoke. But my wife has taken a rather more deliberate and critical examination of my habit, limiting me to certain rooms in the house, conscious that it is not just a question of a filthy habit but a dangerous one, a habit that certainly should not be encouraged. It is an addiction. There can be no doubt about that. It is an addiction that is shared by a great many Canadians. Roughly one-third of Canadians smoke. They spend something in the order of 1.2 per cent of the Gross National Product on their habit. I should say it is we smokers who spend that amount of money. It is an interesting figure because it turns out to be just about the money that we spend on scientific research.
When one considers the over-all cost of the health system and so on I think it can be fairly claimed that with the amount of money that tobacco smoking costs the population, Governments are more than enough compensated for the needed expenditures required by the country in the area of scientific research. Some 30,000 people die-and I note here that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre, suggested that 300,000 people died per year from smoking. I am not even sure that that many people per annum die; but certainly 30,000 people die as a result of indulging in the habit. Increasingly, evidence demonstrates that approximately 1,000 people become victims of indirect smoking. Thus we are faced with the reality that an increasing proportion of the population which condemns smoking are being affected by it and want to see the habit eliminated. That includes many smokers. I must confess I have a compact with my son that will determine in specific terms when I will have to take hold of the issue and abandon my $3-a-day habit.
When one considers all of the issues involved, when one considers the costs involved, and when one considers the discomfort caused to non-smokers there can be nothing clearer in terms of what should be done if we are to take a significant step forward in improving the state of the health of the people of Canada. Undoubtedly, the single most important step that we can take would be to pass legislation such as that tabled by my colleague. Parenthetically, I say that my colleague has been an effective educator in this respect.
Whatever we may want to consider with respect to caveats, whatever we might want to take into account with respect to the situation of the smoker, the emphasis must be on the nonsmoker and the termination of this habit which has the dimensions of a national habit to so many. It may well be that
Non-Smokers' Health Act
as the Hon. Member for Capilano has indicated, there has to be a great deal of care in drafting the final form of this legislation. I agree that in committee, perhaps, it will be necessary to take into account that if we are to solve this major problem we also have to in some measure take into account the great difficulty involved in imposing sharp and rapid change upon a certain portion of the population which by and large consists of people who have grown up smoking. But these are details. I see no proper place in this debate for examining very closely those details because the principle of this legislation is clear. If we are to change the smoking habits of the nation, if we are to provide the single most important change in respect of improving the health of Canadians, then this legislation should gain the support of the House.
Let us remind ourselves of what it would do. It would have the Government do what it could easily do itself by virtue of introducing legislation. I think it is unfortunate that it was necessary that a Private Member provide the initiative that the Government lacks. Essentially, what this Bill would do is to amend the Hazardous Products Act so that tobacco would be classified under that Act as a hazardous product. This would provide for the regulation of advertisement, importation, sales and so on of tobacco products. It would have the effect of ensuring that tobacco products be clearly labelled to be dangerous to one's health.
I must relate to Hon. Members an experience that I had just recently. I was trying to chose, as a smoker, a package of cigarettes that had a low tar and nicotine content as compared to others. I know that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood, would say that that is a silly exercise. But, after all, I am a victim. I could not read the label. It was not a question of looking at this item, smoker or not, and having provided to me a clear indication that this is a dangerous substance. It was impossible to determine anything that was written on the label. Certainly, if anything, it is elementary. What could be more elementary than making it clearly known to all who would engage in the habit, or might be tempted to engage in the activity, that tobacco, cigarettes, are a dangerous product to one's health?
This Bill would also provide a guarantee to workers that they would be able to work in a smoke-free environment. What could be more elementary than that? Surely, it is necessary to make arrangements to let down softly those who are addicted to nicotine. That is a detail. But there can be no doubt that this House ought to pass a Bill-and I hope the other place will give its consent-that there should be provided to all of those working under federal jurisdiction, whether they are standing still, moving across the sea or through the sky, a smoke-free environment. Travellers on common carriers ought to be provided circumstances in which tobacco smoke will not be either an irritant or a threat.
So this is a Bill that is simple in its premise. It is clear in its purpose. Its justification is abundantly found in the danger that tobacco smoke poses to me, to other smokers and to those

March 31, 1987
Non-Smokers' Health Act
who must breathe the air that I create by virtue of my bad habit.

Mr. Speaker, as a smoker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the Bill before the House. 1 admit that smoking can be dangerous. Any sensible person will understand that. For instance, if you eat steak three times a day, it might not be very good for your health either.
Mr. Speaker, cigarette smoke is not only bad for the smoker's health but also for that of non-smokers. More and more Canadians are starting to realize this. Scientific findings on side-stream smoke were recently published in a report by Everett Koop, the U.S. Surgeon General, who discussed the effetcs of side-stream smoke on non-smokers.
Tobacco smoke contains particles and gaseous products which in turn contain more than 60 substances that may cause cancer and other diseases. According to the Surgeon General's report, the smoke from the burning end of a cigarette contains more toxic products and cancer-causing substances than the smoke inhaled and exhaled by the smoker. In fact, many studies have concluded that the risk of lung cancer for the non-smoker is increased by 30 per cent as a result of exposure to side-stream smoke.
The combination of smoke produced by a lighted cigarette and the smoke exhaled by a smoker puts the lives of these involuntary smokers at risk.
When parents smoke, it increases the risk of complications during the pregnancy, including low-birth weight and a higher rate of stillbirths. The children of smokers are also more prone to bronchitis and pneumonia than children of non-smokers. Upper respiratory infections are more frequent and there is also a grater risk that they will get some kind of cancer later on.
Mr. Speaker, in a recent report on the environment on board aircraft, the U.S. National Academy of Science identified the danger of the effects of smoke in aircraft and recommended that the U.S. Congress considerer prohibiting smoking in aircraft and on public transit. In a subsequent report, the Academy also concluded that the risk of lung cancer was increased for non-smokers when they were exposed to tobacco smoke. Similarly, the Academy indicated that children exposed to side-stream smoke were more likely to get upper-respiratory and lung infections.
From scientific research on smoking and the health of nonsmokers, we can draw three general conclusions:
"Involuntary smoking is a cause of disease, including lung cancer, among non-smokers.
Children of smokers suffer more frequently from respiratory illnesses and symptoms compared with children of nonsmokers. The lung capacity of children of smokers develops at a slower rate.
Separating smokers from non-smokers on the same premises may reduce but does not altogether eliminate the problem of exposure to side-stream smoke."
Now that the Canadian public is becoming informed of the dangers of smoking and the risk incurred by passive smokers, it has been urging many changes with respect to the use of tobacco products in public places.
Across Canada, smoke-free public places, work places and public transit are being designated. Municipal and provincial Governments as well as labour and management are working very hard to change policies on smoking in closed premises.
The smoker's rights are questioned when smoking increases the risk of disease for those occupying the same environment. Today, our Government is subsidizing non-governmental organizations such as the Canadian Lung Association and the Canadian Cancer Society which are actively promoting a smoke-free society. In fact, these medical and public health interest groups play a very important role in changing the attitude of society to smoking, and that is why we intend to continue to support their efforts.
Furthermore, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) recently proposed a new regulation prohibiting smoking on domestic and transborder flights of two hours or less on Canadian aircraft. Most major Canadian cities are setting restrictions on smoking in public places and are gradually adopting increasingly stricter bylaws in this respect. For instance, one bylaw put into effect recently in Vancouver has restricted the number of areas where smoking is allowed in most public buildings in that city, including office buildings. If people working in an office are unable to agree on the issue of smoking at work, the office automatically becomes a nonsmoking area. Smoking is also prohibited in taxis, retail stores, at service counters and in line-ups.
This year, Quebec also adopted legislation restricting smoking in public places. It is the first provincial legislation of its kind. The Quebec legislation consists of two components: the first prohibits smoking or restricts smoking to certain designated areas in Government buildings, hospitals, educational institutions, public transit and many other public buildings. In the second part, municipalities are empowered to pass additional bylaws in this respect within their respective jurisdictions.
In Canada today, several transportation modes, one province, 40 municipalities and thousands of work places and public places have adopted policies to protect non-smokers from side-stream smoke. This is a social trend that is becoming increasingly widespread and will bring us ever closer to the ultimate objective of a great many Canadians, namely that Canada will be a smoke-free country by the year 2000!

Mr. Speaker, I want to join in the debate on Bill C-204, standing in the name of the
March 31, 1987

Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), and to speak in favour of this Private Members' Bill.
We often hear stories in respect of those who smoke. One time someone said that if God wanted us to smoke, he would have put chimneys where our heads are. I agree with those who say that smoking is not natural to the human species. In fact, when we really think about it and consider the nicotine and charcoal taken into our bodies, we can imagine that they are not very good for our health.
There was a time when we thought that smoking made us more confident. When we were young we put cigarettes in our mouths, lit them up, and thought that it gave us a certain ambiance, confidence, or grown-up approach to life.
We now know differently. All the evidence is in. There is no doubt. It all points to the fact that smoking is a definite health hazard, not only for those who smoke, but for the innocent, those who do not smoke and are in the presence of smokers.
Bill C-204 is an eminently wise Bill. What does it do? First, it bans promotion and advertising of tobacco. Second, it gives Canadian travellers the right to smoke-free air on common carriers. Third, it guarantees in federally regulated operations that workers have the right to smoke-free work sites.
Bill C-204 has support. The list of its supporters is indeed very impressive; very impressive groups and individuals support the enactment of the Bill. The Canadian Cancer Society supports it. The Lung Association supports it. The Canadian Medical Association supports it. Other regional health groups support it, such as the Manitoba Medical Association and the Medical Society of Nova Scotia.
Many Hon. Members who have spoken so far support the Bill. Previously we heard a colleague who is a smoker support the Bill. Unions representing workers support the Bill. I have in my hand a letter dated March 25, 1987, and directed to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood. It reads:
Dear Ms. McDonald:
You can count on the support of the Airline Division of CUPE for Bill C-
204.
I will be in Ottawa on April 9 and could meet with you to discuss how the
Airline Division of CUPE may contribute further to help Bill C-204 become
law.
It is signed by Richard Nowlan, Division President of Local 4004 of CUPE. I recall sitting many times in the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration when it considered amendments to Part IV of the Canada Labour Code concerning occupational health and safety. When we considered changes to that part of the Canada Labour Code, we gave workers the right to refuse work in conditions which they considered injurious to their health.
There is a grave concern in the workplace in respect of all the new untested chemicals which come on the market. Workers may not know the contents of the chemicals or what their effects will be on their health. There is a consciousness now, and efforts are being made to ensure that the contents are clearly identified. In fact, workers can obtain from computer
Non-Smokers' Health Act
systems instant information about chemicals in the workplace and their health implications. That information is available to them.
All the evidence is clear on this one particular substance. It is a killer. However, we have not moved to ensure that workers can work in an environment free of second-hand smoke or the effects of smoking themselves.
We have not had the courage to follow up on what we now know is a danger to human health. We have not moved on it. The Bill would move us in that direction. No reasonable worker who would say that cigarettes are a dangerous substance would say that the Government should not ensure the health of workers on the job. It is something for which workers and their representatives have been fighting in provincial and federal labour legislation to ensure a healthy working environment.
I should now like to deal with tobacco advertising because the Bill would in fact ban it. I suspect that the Government from time to time has shown a reluctance to move on banning tobacco advertising and to encourage Canadians to give up smoking or not start it. It is a trend today that Canadians at a younger and younger age are developing the habit of smoking.
I think the Government has become dependent upon tobacco usage, upon smoking. It has been reluctant to give up the smoking habit because it sees it as generating tax revenues. In every Budget since I have been around the House cigarettes have always been the favourite target. With every penny increase in the tax on cigarettes, the Government becomes more and more dependent upon income from tobacco.
As a matter of fact, the revenues collected by federal, provincial, and territorial Governments from tobacco sales amount to $3.03 billion per year. Of course the Government does not recognize that it is offset by costs in health care services.
The matter was brought home to me when I took a heart attack last summer. When I arrived at emergency in the hospital, the first question asked was: "Do you smoke?" When I said "no", there was relief on the face of those attending me.
We must think of the health care costs, the costs in absenteeism, and the costs in fire damage. They are estimated at $8 billion. The Government should recognize the false economy- approximately $3 billion are collected in taxes but over $8 billion are paid out in costs. The Government has everything to gain by phasing out and trying to encourage Canadians to quit the smoking habit.
The third area in the Bill concerns the right to travel in a smoke-free environment. I can only come to Ottawa by air, train, or bus, and I must be here. When I do so, I am trusting that the bus, plane, or train will be driven safely. My health is in the hands of those conducting the system. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I have no protection from second-hand smoke. As a matter of fact, you can smoke in the rear seats of buses but the air gets circulated to the front of the bus.

March 31, 1987
Royal Assent
SO)
I think it makes a lot of sense for travellers on common carriers that airplanes, trains, and buses be smoke-free, I want to urge Members of this House with all the vigour that I can to support Bill C-204 because it is wise and healthy to do so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Price (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the purposes of Bill C-204 is to regulate smoking in federal workplaces. The employees in these buildings and facilities are or will soon be subject to the Canada Labour Code which is administered by Labour Canada. Therefore, I want to take a few moments of the time of the House to elaborate on the provisions found in the code relating to occupational health and safety.
The Canada Labour Code consists of a number of parts of which Part IV is of interest to the House at this time. Part IV of the Canada Labour Code applies to federal works, undertakings and businesses and certain Crown corporations, and provides for the occupational safety and health of the employees of these establishments. Specific examples of federal works, undertakings and businesses include the federal Public Service, banks, radio and television stations, railway shops and grain elevators. When the code is extended to apply to operation of trains, aircraft and ships in the near future, it will apply to the employees in almost all the workplaces where the proposed Act should and would apply.
The purpose of the code is to prevent accidents and injury arising out of or occurring in the course of employment to which the code applies. It achieves this by requiring the employer to ensure that the safety and health of every person employed by the employer is protected while at work.
The Canada occupational safety and health regulation issued pursuant to the code prescribes the minimum standards that the employer must meet in order to comply with the code. Part X of the regulations addresses dangerous substances. A dangerous substance is defined as a hazardous substance or a chemical, physical or biological agent that because of a property it possesses is hazardous to the safety or health of a person exposed to it. Part X requires that when there is a likelihood that an employee may be exposed to a dangerous substance, the substance must be identified and its exposure quantified and compared to a permissible limit. Tobacco smoke contains literally thousands of potentially dangerous substances. They range from simple substances such as carbon dioxide to the more dangerous poisons such as carbon monoxide. Packages of American cigarettes specifically warn the smoker of the carbon monoxide hazard.
Under the Canada Labour Code, if a non-smoker were to complain about being exposed to the tobacco smoke from a colleague, the exposure of the non-smoker to specific constituents of the smoke would have to exceed the established permissible limits before it could be determined if the employer is in violation of the code. If the worker were exposed to more than the allowable concentration of a specific compound, the employer would be required to reduce the exposure to
acceptable values or face a fine or even imprisonment. The fines under the code vary depending upon the severity of the contravention and range up to $100,000 where the contravention results in the death or serious injury of an employee. The maximum prison term is two years for a wilful contravention which results in a death or serious injury.
The code also permits employees to refuse to work if they have reasonable cause to believe-

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-CLEAN-UP OF NIAGARA RIVER AND LAKE ONTARIO
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-CLEAN-UP OF NIAGARA RIVER AND LAKE ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is a very special day. It is March 31, 1987. That may not mean an awful lot to you, Mr. Speaker. In fact, as you think about it, perhaps all it means is that it is the end of the month of March. Perhaps you are thinking that it is pay-day. I suspect there might be a ray of light which brightens you at that thought.
March 31, 1987

However, while it may not mean an awful lot to you, to the five million or more people who inhabit the area around the Niagara River, Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence River, it is a red-letter day because today and from now on there should be less toxic chemicals going into the water they drink than there has ever been before. Today marks the end of one year of sampling. From April 1, 1986, until March 31, 1987, there was sampling of the water in the Niagara River for the purpose of establishing a base point over which we hope the quality of the water which people drink from the Niagara River, Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence River will improve.
This is in accordance with a declaration of intent which was signed by four parties: Environment Canada, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Ontario Ministry of the Environment, and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation. It was signed a short time ago with the purpose and intent of ensuring that from now on the toxic pollutants which are going into the Niagara River will be reduced by 50 per cent by the year 1996. In order to monitor that and ensure that it does happen, that declaration of intent calls for reports to be issued to the public every six months.
That is extremely important because it appears that real progress has been made at last in cleaning up the drinking water in Lake Ontario, the Niagara River and the St. Lawrence River. It is important because Canada and the United States have been talking about doing this since 1919. It is important because the chemical dumps on the American side of the Niagara River-particularly those infamous four, Love Canal, Hyde Park, S area dump, and the 102nd Street dump-have been described as the world's largest storehouse of deadly dioxin. It has been leaking into the Niagara River for some time.
This agreement is important because just one two-hundredth of a drop of the worst dioxin, which is 2,3,7,8,-TCDD, can kill a person. Only a shovelful of that dioxin dropped into Lake Ontario could destroy the drinking water of Lake Ontario for all time.
It is also important because we know that the deadly dioxin is leaking out of the dumps along the Niagara River, particularly the Hyde Park dump, where it has been identified as seeping down the face of the gorge right into the river. There are some 900 kilograms, almost a tonne, of that kind of deadly dioxin in the Hyde Park dump alone.
This agreement is important because we know that there are some 70,000 tonnes of other chemical wastes, most of which we have identified as cancer-causing wastes, in that Hyde Park dump alone. It is important because recently, near the mouth of the Petit Flume storm sewer located in Tonawanda, New York, they have identified that deadly dioxin in clams. We know that in this sewer alone is a chemical-laden sediment that would cover a football field to a depth of one metre.
Adjournment Debate
This is an important step and that is why it is such a red-letter day for the people who live around Lake Ontario, the Niagara River and the St. Lawrence River. In spite of all this good news, there are some questions still to be answered. That is why I am delighted to have the Parliamentary Secretary here tonight to answer some of those questions that people have been asking.
For instance, why has the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States not designated these dumps under the American Super Fund legislation? Why has the Occidental Chemical Company that controls and owns these dumps on the American side of the Niagara River spent money to help clean up the Chernobyl accident in the Soviet Union but is not spending money to clean up the chemicals which they themselves own in our own backyard?
Will those chemicals be excavated and the toxic material removed and destroyed, or will there only be some containment plan to try to keep it there on site? Why, in spite of this declaration of intent and the target of reducing by 50 per cent the flow of toxic chemicals into the river, will 4.5 tonnes of pollution still be going into the river every day, even with these clean-up targets?
When will the 45 Ontario industries and the 53 United States industries that are currently polluting the Great Lakes be cleaned up? When will the 10 Ontario hazardous waste sites and the 105 U.S. hazardous waste sites around the Great Lakes be cleaned up? When will the 32 Ontario municipalities and the 81 American municipalities that are still dumping sewage and polluting the Great Lakes be cleaned up?
Those are answers the people of Canada want to know and I am looking forward to getting those answers from the Parliamentary Secretary tonight.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-CLEAN-UP OF NIAGARA RIVER AND LAKE ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) and to acknowledge his enthusiasm for environmental issues, his search for answers and the need for certain measures to be taken. Tonight I will be elaborating on the question brought to the attention of this House by the Hon. Member on February 3. That was in relation to the international declaration of intent relating to the Niagara River Toxic Management Plan.
On behalf of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), I am pleased to provide the Hon. Member with details of that declaration, signed with Mr. Lee Thomas, administrator of the United States Environmental Protection Agency, Mr. Jim Bradley, the Minister of the Environment for Ontario and Mr. Henry Williams of the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation. The occasion of this signing, I might add, was a very successful three day international symposium on toxics in the Niagara, jointly sponsored by these four environmental agencies and held in Toronto.

March 31, 1987
Adjournment Debate
This declaration of intent, which was toasted at the time of signing with pure water, is a statement of political will and commitment of the four jurisdictions to reduce the loadings of toxic chemicals entering the Niagara River by 50 per cent over the coming decade. In order to accomplish this goal, the four governments are committed to undertake and complete all the activities defined in an all-party Niagara River Toxic Management Plan which was released on October 30, 1986.
This plan is a technical document which describes specific work activities and schedules for completing these activities which we agreed to undertake jointly and individually. The plan will be updated and a revised version will be released in July, 1987. In addition, the declaration of intent also requires the four jurisdictions to review and publicly report on the state of new and emerging technologies to protect the environment from threats of hazardous waste landfill sites. The emphasis will be on such techniques as excavation, removal and on-site destruction of contaminated materials. At all chemical dump sites, excavation, removal and destruction will be considered an option.
The signing of this declaration constitutes the result of fruitful negotiations between the four governments and marks our will to offer a healthy and clean environment to every Canadian.

subtopic: REFUGEES-IMMINENT DEATH OF HUNGER STRIKER-(A) GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) PROCESSING OF REFUGEE CLAIMS
REFUGEES-IMMINENT DEATH OF HUNGER STRIKER-(A) GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) PROCESSING OF REFUGEE CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago when the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) announced that the Chileans blocked by him in Argentina were not refugees, that none of those people were refugees, my reaction was not to believe him. I did not believe him because I had personally spoken to a number of Chileans in Montreal who had arrived recently and who were seeking refugee status. They were people I would consider to be refugees. For instance, there was a lawyer who had worked for the Church in Chile and had been arrested several times. He finally decided to leave his country because he feared for his life.
There was a truck driver whose friends had taken part in demonstrations and who was therefore implicated through his association with these people. He too feared for his life and decided to leave his country. In the group in Montreal, at least among those I spoke to, there are people I consider to be refugees because I felt their stories had the ring of truth.
When the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) said a few weeks ago that no one in Argentina was a refugee, I reached the conclusion that his assessment was not credible and that at least some of these people had a legitimate claim.
If the Minister had said that 20 or 25 were refugees, maybe half, I would have thought his assessment was credible. But when he says that no one is a refugee, I protest.
Since that time the facts have confirmed my feeling. Last week, the Quebec Minister of Immigration, after evaluating about 50 people, reached the conclusion that at least 10 of the people in question were in sufficiently precarious circumstances to be admitted to Quebec on humanitarian grounds. The Minister asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration to review those cases. I would like to point out that only those who asked to be allowed to settle in Quebec were evaluated by the Government of Quebec.
Then, Mr. Speaker, what has been the response of the Minister of Employment and Immigration? He says he is puzzled about the various assessments. You will admit Mr. Speaker that the Minister is disarming by naive. This confusing situation would justify a form decision on his part. He may have 56,000 assessments, Mr. Speaker, but the only one which really matters is his own, because he is the one who may admit these refugees in Canada. He is the only one who decides whether or not they have the right to enter this country.
Such a decision being so crucial and final-for this people it is a matter of life and death-it is imperative to ensure that those who are seeking refugee status may do so with a minimum of legal protection.
This is why recommendations made to the Government in recent years have been unanimous. People are asking for an independent, neutral and impartial procedure. Department of Immigration officials should not be expected to decide the fate of refugees because their responsibility is to administer the Immigration Act. These applications should be examined by people who are expert in refugee matters, and the Department of Immigration should not have anything to do with the whole process.
When applications are filed abroad .. . For example, the Chileans who have made headlines in recent weeks, who have been detained in Argentina, left stranded in Argentina by the Minister, these people in foreign countries are often in a predicament, separated from their families, facing an official who may not feel much sympathy for refugees, they have no access to legal advice, they have absolutely no right to appeal, they are at the mercy of the Minister of Immigration and his officials.
I therefore urge the Minister to admit that the refugee determination process in foreign lands has serious drawbacks. The Government should repeal the shameful measures imposed last February 20 and set up a compassionate and fair treatment system for refugees.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: REFUGEES-IMMINENT DEATH OF HUNGER STRIKER-(A) GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) PROCESSING OF REFUGEE CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the Hon.
March 31, 1987

Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) to the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) on March 4, 1987.
On March 12, 1987, the Government decided, for humanitarian and compassionate reasons, to bring three wives and their children to Canada to join their husbands. The Minister's permits were issued, and they arrived at Mirabel on Saturday, March 14, 1987.
As for the remainder of the group, each has been interviewed by our officers at the Canadian Embassy in Buenos Aires. They have also been seen by a Quebec immigration officer.
On the basis of their interviews, our foreign service officers had initially concluded that none of the group fled Chile for reasons of persecution; rather, they were coming to Canada for economic reasons. However, we have received additional information from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees' representative in Argentina, and it is the conclusion of the Canadian officials that two persons have valid claims to be Convention Refugees.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees provides information and advice, but it is only the Canadian Government which can decide the validity of a refugee claim from someone seeking to enter Canada.
Under the Cullen-Couture Agreement with the Quebec Government, the Quebec Immigration Minister, Louise Robic, has the legal means to bring to Canada, as independent immigrants, any of the Chileans in the group remaining in Argentina.
Mme. Robic announced on March 30, 1987, that the nine Chileans granted permission to enter Quebec shall be processed as independent immigrants, including standard medical and background checks, before they can be brought forward. The remaining Chileans can, should they wish to do so, apply to the Canadian Embassy to determine whether they can meet the selection standards for immigrants other than Convention refugees.
Canada remains open to genuine refugees from Chile. However, many of the people coming from that country recently using the in-transit route have in fact been economic migrants or family class applicants joining relatives here. These people must be dealt with in the normal way and must not be allowed to short-circuit the immigration system, or jump the queue.
Canada has an ongoing immigration program from Chile. Last year, 453 Chileans entered the country under regular immigration programs. Canada has an outstanding record with respect to receiving refugees from Chile. Since the fall of the Allende regime in September, 1973, Canada has admitted 16,735 people from that country.

subtopic: FINANCE-SALES TAX CREDIT PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR GREATER PUBLICITY
FINANCE-SALES TAX CREDIT PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR GREATER PUBLICITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) reminded us that it was March 31, and he did so because he had a particular interest in that date. What I want to speak about today also reminds me that it is March 31, which means that tomorrow we are into the month of April, by the end of which we must have our income tax returns filed. Now is the time to be thinking about preparing our income tax returns.
Last week, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) about the federal sales tax credit that was introduced in the February 1986 Budget. This is a terrific program. Its purpose is to take into account the increase in federal sales tax while making sure that lower income Canadians are not penalized.
Because it is a new program, I have found that a lot of people who are eligible for it do not know about it. For that reason, I should like to take a few minutes to explain what the program is.
It is a tax credit program, and under it those with an income of less than $15,000 would be eligible for a tax credit of $50. For a family whose combined income is less than $15,000, a husband and wife who were living together as of the end of last year would be eligible for a tax credit of $100, plus $25 for each child.
This is a significant amount of money for lower income families, and we want to make sure that those who are eligible receive it. The point is, in order to get the credit, one has to file an income tax return. There are a number of people in this category whose incomes are such that they do not ordinarily pay any income tax and therefore do not file an income tax return.
I should like to refer to what was brought to my attention in my riding of Capilano. Senior citizens whose incomes were basically their old age pension, and perhaps the GIS, who do not ordinarily file income tax returns may not know that this year they should do so because they are probably eligible for the $50 credit. We want to make sure that people know about it.
Another category which has been brought to my attention is that of students. Every Canadian 18 years of age and over who is eligible and has an income of less than $15,000 should be filing an income tax form this year in order to obtain the particular credit.
I asked my question on March 25. I was pleased that the Minister of National Revenue in his usual way immediately issued a press release the next day-and I hope it has been well covered in the media-reminding people to claim their tax credit.

March 31, 1987
Adjournment Debate
As he said in the particular press release: "This tax credit is of particular importance to low-income Canadians, many of whom would not normally have to file a tax return". He emphasized that in order to claim the sales tax credit, a tax return must be filed.
That is the message we want to ensure that we get across. I hope all Hon. Members of the House will make the effort, through press releases and householders to their constituents, to ensure that the message gets out.
There is another point I want to raise because it was brought to my attention. There is some concern about people who have never filed tax returns. They are not used to it, they might be scared about it, and they do not know where to go for help. First I would advise them not to go to tax discounters. I was very pleased with the legislation we brought in last year to limit the role of tax discounters. It is not worth it, because there is help out there.
In my own riding of Capilano, British Columbia, I have worked with north shore seniors' groups and the information centre. In particular, the north shore health and information service provides volunteers to help seniors fill out their income tax returns. This is probably true across the country. There are many volunteers who will go to the homes of senior citizens and be in community centres to help with tax returns.
I was delighted by an article which was brought to my attention. It indicated that this kind of service was being offered by the Department of National Revenue. The particular project in Sydney, Nova Scotia seems to be an ideal one. I hope it is done right across the country. In the article Mr. Ross Crewe, Public Relations Manager for the Sydney District Office of Revenue Canada, talked about a program where Revenue Canada recruited all sorts of volunteers in the community to help people prepare their tax returns. If someone phones up, they will send a volunteer to the homes of seniors to help them. It does not have to be a scary kind of situation. It has some 70 volunteers in Sydney working out of a store-front office, so it is accessible. People do not have to climb a lot of stairs or go into a government office, which might be a little scary.
I should like to refer to some of the comments of people who have used the service. A gentleman, Mr. John Briand, said:
They say filling out the form is simple but it can be complicated . .. The
volunteers know just how to fill it out, and it's a lot easier for them to figure-
Kristene Brown, a University College of Cape Breton student is not taking any chances. She said:
I wanted to make sure I'd get it done right.
She had gone for that kind of help too. That kind of help is available.
I urge low-income Canadians-and we expect that 75,000 Canadian families will be eligible for the federal sales tax credit-to make sure that they get their forms in. If by chance they miss out or know of someone who has missed out, they will have a chance even after the end of April this year. They
will have three years within which to claim the credit. Of course, $50 in the hand is better than $50 waiting out there.
I encourage the Minister, his Department, and all colleagues to make extra special efforts this year to ensure that Canadians are aware of this excellent program which the Government has put in place. It shows our care and compassion for Canadians who are having to make do on lower incomes.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Jennifer Cossitt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: FINANCE-SALES TAX CREDIT PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR GREATER PUBLICITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I respond to my colleague's question of March 25 regarding the public awareness of the federal sales tax credit. I commend her for her ongoing concern and compassion on behalf of all Canadians.
As you are no doubt aware, some four million Canadians can benefit from this Government initiative. I would like to assure all Members that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) is energetic in promoting and informing Canadians how to claim this valuable credit.
The federal tax credit is progressive. It permits eligible Canadians to receive a fully refundable credit of $50 for themselves, an additional $50 for their spouse and $25 per qualified relative. Not only is this a progressive measure by virtue of the fact that it is refundable, this credit is sensitive to the needs of low-income Canadians and gradually diminishes as a taxpayer's income increases. This credit is designed to help achieve the Government's objective of tax equity.
Department personnel have been mobilized across Canada to promote the availability of this credit through the Department's volunteer program, a program that assisted some 85,000 low-income tax filers last year. Positive results of their efforts are recorded in numerous news articles, articles which themselves stress the importance of filing a tax return in order to claim the federal sales tax credit.
The Minister of National Revenue recently issued a news release reminding Canadians of the eligibility criteria for this credit. In addition, the Minister will shortly be issuing a letter to all Members of Parliament and Senators urging them to publicize this credit in their constituencies. An article explaining the credit and how it is to be claimed will be enclosed with the letters so that Members of Parliament and Senators can provide copies to community papers and community groups right across Canada. I urge all members to use this opportunity to reach out to their constituents.
Not only has this Government introduced a progressive tax measure with this credit, we are conscientiously promoting the credit with those very Canadians for whom it was introduced. I would stress, Mr. Speaker, that throughout the remainder of the tax filing system, the Department will continue to explore all available channels for publicizing this important new credit.
The Minister believes that most Canadians who are eligible for the federal sales tax credit are aware of how to claim for it in their tax return. But, I want to remind my colleagues that
March 31, 1987

there are provisions in the Income Tax Act for claiming this and other credits in future years should an individual overlook the availability of a credit this year. This provision gives tax filers up to three years to make claims that they may have missed.
I appreciate this opportunity to bring to the attention of Hon. Members the steps being taken by Revenue Canada, Taxation, to ensure that Canadians take full advantage of this new refundable credit.
